opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think if you step back and look at the history, America has actually been remarkably good at this, and the basic recipe is simple: we let innovation flourish, but when a technology is powerful enough to cause serious harm, we put in place safety standards that companies have to meet *before* they sell their product to the public.

Think about pharmaceuticals. Before the FDA really had teeth, you had things like thalidomide causing terrible birth defects in other countries, and the response was to say: if you want to sell a new drug, the burden is on you to show it's safe and effective. Not on the government to prove it's dangerous after people get hurt. Same with aviation. You can't just build a new airliner and start flying passengers; the FAA has to sign off. Same with cars, food, nuclear power plants. We've done this over and over.

And crucially, this hasn't killed innovation. It's arguably what made these industries thrive, because people trust them. You get on a plane without worrying about it. You take medicine your doctor prescribes. Safety standards created the trust that created the markets.

What's so striking to me about AI is that it's the glaring exception. Right now, in the United States, there are more regulations on selling a sandwich than on building potentially superhuman AI. A sandwich shop has to pass a health inspection. An AI company can release a system it openly says could pose catastrophic risks, and there's essentially no binding requirement to demonstrate it's safe first.

So when people frame this as "regulation versus innovation," I think that's a false choice. The traditional American approach is to treat powerful technologies like every other powerful technology: clear safety standards, set independently, that you have to meet before deployment. That's not radical. That's just being consistent with what we've always done. The radical thing would be to carve out the most powerful technology in human history as the one industry that gets to skip all that.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes safety standards required before deployment as the traditional approach; it does not state that liability is the first response to demonstrated harms.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention chatbot companies facing common-law claims or allege that chatbots caused physical harm.

fable-5.1.text:
The way I think about it is that the United States has actually had a pretty consistent approach for over a century, and it's basically this: if you want to sell something that could hurt people, you have to show it's safe before you sell it. Not the other way around.

Take the FDA. Before you can sell a new drug, you have to run clinical trials, you have to convince regulators that the benefits outweigh the risks, and only then do you get to market. We do the same with airplanes. Boeing doesn't get to just fly a new plane full of passengers and see what happens. The FAA has to certify it first. Same with bridges, same with nuclear reactors, same with cars, same with food. The burden of proof is on the person who wants to put the product out there, not on the public to prove it's dangerous after it's already killed somebody.

And the reason we do this isn't because Americans hate innovation. It's the opposite. We do it because that's how you get innovation that people actually trust. When the FDA was created, the pharmaceutical industry didn't collapse. It thrived, because people stopped being afraid that the medicine would poison them. Safety standards are what let the biotech industry become a massive success story. Aviation is the safest form of travel we've ever invented precisely because we regulated it so carefully.

So what strikes me as bizarre is that AI is, right now, basically the one powerful technology where we've thrown that whole tradition out the window. You can go to a sandwich shop in San Francisco and face more safety regulation than you do if you're building a system you yourself claim might one day be smarter than every human on Earth. The companies are allowed to just release it and we all find out together what happens. There are no safety standards at all. That's not the American tradition. That's the exception.

And I'd argue it's a very recent exception, driven mostly by lobbying and by this narrative that any rule at all will hand the future to China. I don't buy that. I think if we simply applied the same standard we apply to drugs and airplanes, you'd have to demonstrate to some competent body that your system is safe and controllable before you deploy it, and then you'd have exactly the kind of healthy, competitive, trusted industry we've managed to build everywhere else. That's not anti-technology. That's just how America has always done it when the stakes are high.

r001.rationale: The response describes premarket safety certification as the traditional approach, not the liability system as the first response to demonstrated harms.

astra-6.text: The traditional American approach is that you’re free to innovate, but you’re not free to hurt people without consequences. You can start a company and develop a new technology, but if your product harms someone, you can be sued. That liability gives companies an incentive to invest in safety, rather than keeping the profits while leaving everyone else to bear the costs. So innovation and accountability go together.

sol-6.1.text: I think the traditional American approach has been to let people innovate, but hold them accountable if they cause harm. You have a lot of freedom to build things and start companies, but that freedom doesn’t mean you get to impose unlimited risks on everybody else. If your product injures someone, you can be sued. And where the consequences are serious enough, we also have safety requirements before you put the product on the market. So it’s a combination of innovation, liability, and safeguards.
